newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Boots aims for loyalty sales boost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Boots aims for loyalty sales boost.

text.p: Britain's biggest pharmacist Boots Co Plc on Wednesday joined the loyalty card stakes with the nationwide launch of its Advantage Card, which the retailer hopes will boost sales and pay for itself in two years.

The card, available from September 1, will cost Boots 52 million pounds ($84.5 million) over three years, but is expected to deliver a four percent sales increase by the end of the 1998/99 financial year. Boots The Chemists sales last year totalled 3.3 billion pounds.
The firm's decision to start a loyalty scheme follows moves by three of Britain's big four food superstores, including Tesco Plc and J. Sainsbury Plc, to introduce loyalty cards.

Customers signing up for the Boots card will receive one point worth one pence, for every 25 pence spent in Boots The Chemists. The points can be redeemed against a range of 10,000 health and beauty products and services sold by the company.
Tesco's Clubcard, the first of these schemes, helped the retailer steal market leadership from rival Sainsbury.
Boots expects more than eight million of its customers to sign up to the card by September 1998 based on two regional trials running since October 1995.

The card will carry a computer chip, giving Boots the capacity to develop a high-quality information database on shopping patterns. Boots said this was more powerful than traditional market research or existing point of sale systems data.
Boots the Chemist managing director Steve Russell said in a statement: "We believe that the Advantage Card will become Britain's largest loyalty scheme."
Russell said Boots believed the loyalty card could raise the average amount spent in Boots by about one third.
He said the average transaction was currently 6.11 pounds, but trials in East Anglia and the south west of England showed the card did increase shoppers' average spending when they visited the store.
"I think the average spend on the Advantage card is about 30 percent higher," he told Reuters by telephone.
Phil Douty, head of customer communications, estimated the sales boost would translate into gross profit of 109 million pounds.
"Over the three-year period the gross profit accruing from the incremental sales is 109 million pounds.....before all the expenses," he said.
The company said the card would pay for itself by the end of the next financial year and Boots would have recovered its investment costs as well as the operating costs on the scheme.
Russell said the card should encourage regular customers either to visit the shops more often or buy more slightly-higher priced items.
"There are also some customers where we don't have as much loyalty as we would like and we're pulling them into the net," he said.
The card would also allow Boots to build up a highly detailed database from purchases made by individual customers.
"The prime benefit is that we are now able to put a name against the...store receipts," Douty said.
He said this would be valuable for evaluating product launches and the impact of new marketing campaigns.
The investment in marketing, database, and training will be 25 million pounds this year, falling to 14 million next year and 13 million in 1999/2000.
Boots shares were two pence higher at 773 pence, after falling about four pence immediately after news of the card launch. -- London Newsroom + 44 171 542 7717 ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
